claim: Impairments in choosing optimally between immediate and delayed rewards are associated with numerous psychiatric disorders.
source: Impairments in choosing optimally between immediate and delayed rewards are associated with numerous psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific literature on intertemporal choice and psychiatric disorders.

claim: Females showed markedly greater preference than males for small, immediate over large, delayed rewards (greater impulsive choice).
source: Females showed markedly greater preference than males for small, immediate over large, delayed rewards (greater impulsive choice).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 2A showing sex differences in choice behavior.

claim: The sex difference in impulsive choice was neither due to differences in food motivation or reward magnitude perception, nor was it affected by estrous cycle.
source: This difference was neither due to differences in food motivation or reward magnitude perception, nor was it affected by estrous cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ad libitum feeding experiments (Figure 4) and estrous cycle tracking (Figure 2B).

claim: Ovariectomies did not affect choice in females.
source: Ovariectomies did not affect choice in females
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing pre- and post-ovariectomy performance shown in Figure 5.

claim: Orchiectomies increased impulsive choice in males.
source: whereas orchiectomies increased impulsive choice in males.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing pre- and post-orchiectomy performance shown in Figure 6.

claim: Male rats exhibit less impulsive choice than females and this difference is at least partly maintained by testicular hormones.
source: These data show that male rats exhibit less impulsive choice than females and that this difference is at least partly maintained by testicular hormones.
evidence: This claim synthesizes the experimental findings from sex comparison and gonadectomy experiments.

claim: Differences in impulsive choice could be linked to gender differences across multiple neuropsychiatric conditions.
source: These differences in impulsive choice could be linked to gender differences across multiple neuropsychiatric conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential implications of the findings.

claim: Intertemporal decision making associates with many neuropsychiatric conditions.
source: One aspect of behavior that associates with many neuropsychiatric conditions is intertemporal decision making (Heerey et al., 2007; Bickel et al., 2012; Bickel et al., 2014; Steinglass et al., 2012; Wilbertz et al., 2013; Hoptman, 2015; Steward et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Individuals choose large over small rewards in the absence of delays but will discount the value of the large rewards as a function of the delay before their delivery.
source: Individuals choose large over small rewards in the absence of delays but will discount the value of the large rewards as a function of the delay before their delivery.
evidence: This describes a well-established behavioral phenomenon in decision-making research.

claim: Greater impulsive choice associates with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
source: For example, an inability to forgo immediate rewards in favor of larger rewards delivered in the future, or greater 'impulsive choice', associates with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (Wilbertz et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Greater impulsive choice associates with substance use disorders.
source: For example, an inability to forgo immediate rewards in favor of larger rewards delivered in the future, or greater 'impulsive choice', associates with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (Wilbertz et al., 2013) and substance use disorders (Bickel et al., 2012; Bickel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A hallmark feature of anorexia nervosa is a maladaptive preference for delayed gratification.
source: In contrast, a hallmark feature of the eating disorder anorexia nervosa is a maladaptive preference for delayed gratification (Steinglass et al., 2012; Steward et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Males exhibit higher rates of impulsive disorders such as substance use and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
source: Notably, the prevalence of these conditions is sex-biased, with males exhibiting higher rates of 'impulsive' disorders (e.g., substance use, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Females exhibit disproportionate rates of anorexia nervosa.
source: and females exhibiting disproportionate rates of anorexia nervosa (Rolls et al., 1991; Becker et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some studies in humans report that males show greater impulsive choice than females.
source: Some studies in humans report that males show greater impulsive choice than females (Kirby and Maraković, 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Some studies in humans report that females show greater impulsive choice than males.
source: whereas others report the opposite (Logue and Anderson, 2001; Reynolds et al., 2006; Smith and Hantula, 2008; Beck and Triplett, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some studies in humans report a lack of gender differences in impulsive choice.
source: or a lack of gender differences altogether (Mischel and Underwood, 1974; Kirby and Maraković, 1995; Silverman, 2003; Bembenutty, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some studies in rodents report no sex differences in impulsive choice.
source: Studies in rodents have been equally inconclusive, with findings ranging from no sex differences (Perry et al., 2008; Eubig et al., 2014; Sackett et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some studies in rodents report males being more impulsive than females.
source: to males being more impulsive than females (Panfil et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Some studies in rodents report females being more impulsive than males.
source: to females being more impulsive than males (Van Haaren et al., 1988; Perry et al., 2007; Weafer and de Wit, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Testosterone and estrogen are the primary hormonal drivers of developmental traits and characteristics in males and females, respectively.
source: Testosterone and estrogen are the primary hormonal drivers of developmental traits and characteristics in males and females, respectively (Wieland et al., 1971; Wilson et al., 1981; Rogol et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Circulating levels of gonadal hormones both during brain development and in fully mature adults can influence a variety of cognitive functions.
source: Circulating levels of these hormones both during brain development and in fully mature adults can influence a variety of cognitive functions (Korol, 2004; Spritzer et al., 2011; Frick et al., 2015; Wagner et al., 2018; Koss and Frick, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Circulating levels of gonadal hormones associate with impulsive choice in both men and women.
source: Studies show that circulating levels of these hormones associate with impulsive choice in both men and women (Takahashi et al., 2006; Doi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Impulsive choice can vary across the menstrual cycle in women.
source: Similarly, impulsive choice can vary across the menstrual cycle in women (Smith et al., 2014; Diekhof, 2015; Stanton, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Exogenous administration of supraphysiological levels of testosterone decreases impulsive choice in male rats.
source: Notably, however, while exogenous administration of supraphysiological levels of testosterone decreases impulsive choice in male rats (Wood et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Testosterone administration at replacement level doses does not affect impulsive choice in humans.
source: this effect is not observed in humans, at least at relatively low (replacement level) doses (Ortner et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Male and female rats did not differ in the numbers of free-choice trials completed in the task.
source: Male and female rats did not differ in the numbers of free-choice trials completed in the task (percentage of trials omitted, t(30) = −1.39, p=0.174).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: All rats reduced their choice of the large reward as the delay to its delivery increased.
source: Moreover, in this experiment and all others reported below, all rats reduced their choice of the large reward as the delay to its delivery increased (main effects of delay, all ps < 0.005).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Females made fewer choices of large, delayed rewards than males.
source: females made fewer choices of large, delayed rewards than males (two-factor ANOVA, main effect of sex: F(1,30)=10.586, p=0.003)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The sex difference in choice was particularly evident when longer delays preceded delivery of the large reward.
source: particularly when longer delays preceded delivery of the large reward (sex × delay interaction: F(4,120)=8.572; p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Choice performance in females was not modulated by estrous cycle phase.
source: Note, however, that choice performance in females was not modulated by estrous cycle phase (main effect of phase: F(3,45)=1.618, p=0.221; phase × delay interaction: F(12,180)=1.765, p=0.168; Figure 2B, see Figure 2—source data 2 for raw data).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Females showed much longer latencies to press the large compared to the small reward lever on forced-choice trials.
source: Consistent with female preference for the small, immediate reward on free-choice trials, females showed much longer latencies to press the large compared to the small reward lever on forced-choice trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and statistical analysis.

claim: Males showed comparable latencies for both small and large reward levers.
source: In contrast, males showed comparable latencies for both levers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and statistical analysis.

claim: Females omitted more forced-choice trials on the large compared to small reward lever, particularly at the longest delays.
source: Follow up analyses for males and females performed separately showed that females omitted more forced-choice trials on the large compared to small reward lever, particularly at the longest delays (main effect of lever: F(1,15)=13.988, p=0.002; lever × delay: F(4,60)=7.526, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Males did not show differences in forced-choice trial omissions between the large and small reward levers.
source: In contrast, no such differences were observed in males (main effect of lever: F(1,15)=2.015, p=0.176; lever × delay: F(4,60)=0.214, p=0.888).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Males and females did not differ in either response latencies or forced-choice trial omissions associated with the small reward lever.
source: In addition, the fact that males and females did not differ in either response latencies or forced-choice trial omissions associated with the small reward lever indicates that females were as motivated as males to perform the task and seek rewards.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on response latencies and trial omissions.

claim: Adult male rats weigh substantially more than females and have greater ad libitum food intake.
source: Adult male rats weigh substantially more than females and have greater ad libitum food intake (Klump et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: One hour ad libitum feeding influenced overall motivation to perform the task.
source: The 1 hr ad libitum schedule influenced overall motivation to perform the task, as evident by a main effect of feeding schedule on the percentage of free-choice trials omitted (F(1,30)=9.115, p=0.005; Figure 4C, see Figure 4—source data 3 for raw data).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The increase in free-choice trial omissions following 1 hour ad libitum feeding was present irrespective of sex.
source: Importantly, however, this increase in free-choice trial omissions was present irrespective of sex (main effect of sex: F(1,30)=0.294, p=0.592; schedule × sex: F(1,30)=0.294, p=0.592).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Sex differences in choice behavior were still present following 1 hour ad libitum feeding.
source: A three-factor repeated measures ANOVA (sex × feeding schedule × delay) performed on choice data showed that the main effects of sex (F(1,23)=26.753, p<0.001) and sex × delay interaction (F(4,92)=11.227, p<0.001; Figure 4A, see Figure 4—source data 1 for raw data) were still present following the 1 hr ad libitum feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: One hour ad libitum feeding significantly decreased choice of large, delayed rewards.
source: In addition, 1 hr ad libitum feeding significantly decreased choice of large, delayed rewards (main effect of feeding schedule: F(1,23)=5.861, p=0.024; Figure 4B, see Figure 4—source data 2 for raw data)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The effect of 1 hour ad libitum feeding on choice behavior was independent of sex.
source: Most importantly, this effect of feeding schedule on choice behavior was independent of sex (schedule × sex: F(1,23)=0.417, p=0.525; schedule × sex × delay: F(4,92)=1.270, p=0.288).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The 24 hour ad libitum schedule influenced overall motivation to perform the task.
source: The 24 hr ad libitum schedule also influenced overall motivation to perform the task as evident by a main effect of feeding schedule on the percentage of free-choice trials omitted (main effect of schedule: F(1,30)=13.400, p=0.001; Figure 4F, see Figure 4—source data 6 for raw data)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Sex differences in choice behavior were still evident following 24 hour ad libitum feeding.
source: A three-factor repeated measures ANOVA (sex × feeding schedule × delay) nevertheless demonstrated main effects of sex (F(1,27)=13.414, p=0.001) as well as a sex × delay interaction (F(4,108)=7.899, p<0.001; Figure 4D, see Figure 4—source data 4 for raw data).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There was no decrease in choice of the large, delayed reward following the 24 hour ad libitum feeding schedule.
source: Unlike the 1 hr ad libitum schedule, there was no decrease in choice of the large, delayed reward following the 24 hr ad libitum feeding schedule (F(1,27)=2.302, p=0.141; schedule × sex: F(1,27)=0.021, p=0.887; schedule × delay: F(4,108)=0.179, p=0.949; schedule × sex × delay: F(4,108)=1.433, p=0.228; Figure 4E, see Figure 4—source data 5 for raw data).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Sex differences in intertemporal choice are not attributable to differences in hunger or food motivation.
source: To summarize, given that robust differences in choice behavior between males and females were still evident following free access to food that was sufficient to reduce rats' motivation to perform the task, these data argue against the sex differences in intertemporal choice being attributable to differences in hunger or food motivation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ad libitum feeding experiments.

claim: Ovariectomy did not affect choice performance in females.
source: A three-factor, repeated measures ANOVA (surgical group [ovariectomy vs. sham] × phase [pre- vs. post-surgery] × delay) was used to analyze the percentage of large reward choices and indicated no main effects or interactions involving ovariectomy (main effect of surgical group: F(1,10)=2.245, p=0.165; main effect of phase: F(1,10)=0.003, p=0.957; surgical group × phase: F(1,10)=0.001, p=0.971; phase × delay: F(4,40)=1.557, p=0.204; surgical group × delay: F(4,40)=1.655, p=0.179; surgical group × phase × delay: F(4,40)=1.698, p=0.170; Figure 5A, see Figure 5—source data 1 for raw data).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ovariectomy did not affect the percentage of trials omitted in females.
source: There were also no effects of phase on the percentage of trials omitted (main effect of phase: F(1,10)=2.390, p=0.153; main effect of surgical group: F(1,10)=2.726, p=0.130; surgical group × phase: F(1,10)=0.850, p=0.378; Figure 5B, see Figure 5—source data 2 for raw data).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ovariectomy did not affect choice performance when tested with shorter delays.
source: A two-factor, repeated measures ANOVA (surgical group × delay) revealed no effects of ovariectomy under the shorter delay set (main effect of surgical group: F(1,8)=0.006, p=0.938; surgical group × delay: F(4,32)=0.407, p=0.802), suggesting that the failure of ovariectomy to influence choice performance was not due insufficient parametric space in which to observe such effects (Figure 5C, see Figure 5—source data 3 for raw data).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Circulating ovarian hormones in adult females do not drive sex differences observed in intertemporal choice.
source: Instead, these data are consistent with the interpretation that circulating ovarian hormones in adult females do not drive sex differences observed in intertemporal choice and are not critical for maintenance of the female-typical pattern of intertemporal choice behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ovariectomy experiments.

claim: Testosterone levels were detectable in sham but not orchiectomized rats.
source: Testosterone levels were detectable in sham but not orchiectomized rats (t(14) = 2.315, p=0.036; sham: 1.892 ng/mL ±0.817 SEM; orchiectomized: 0 ng/mL ±0 SEM).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements of testosterone levels.

claim: Orchiectomy resulted in a significant surgical group × phase × delay interaction in choice behavior.
source: Using a three-factor repeated measures ANOVA, the analysis of choice data (surgical group [orchiectomy vs. sham] × phase [pre- vs. post-surgery] × delay) revealed a trend toward a surgical group × phase interaction (F(1,14)=3.750, p=0.073), and a significant surgical group × phase × delay interaction (F(4,56)=2.569, p=0.048; Figure 6A, see Figure 6—source data 1 for raw data)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Orchiectomized but not sham rats reduced their choice of the large, delayed reward post-surgery compared to pre-surgery conditions.
source: Figure 6B shows that orchiectomized but not sham rats reduced their choice of the large, delayed reward post-surgery compared to pre-surgery conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Orchiectomy showed a trend toward a main effect of phase on choice behavior.
source: These analyses indicated a trend toward a main effect of phase (F(1,7)=4.829, p=0.064; Figure 6B, see Figure 6—source data 2 for raw data)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Orchiectomy resulted in a significant phase × delay interaction such that choice of the large reward decreased post-surgery, particularly at the longest delays.
source: and a significant phase × delay interaction (F(4,28)=3.029, p=0.034) in orchiectomized rats, such that choice of the large reward decreased post-surgery, particularly at the longest delays.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Sham surgery did not affect choice behavior in males.
source: In contrast, there was neither a main effect of phase nor a phase × delay interaction in sham rats (main effect of phase: F(1,7)=0.138, p=0.722; phase × delay: F(4,28)=0.407, p=0.687).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Orchiectomy did not influence the percentage of free-choice trials omitted.
source: Finally, orchiectomy did not influence the percentage of free-choice trials omitted (main effect of surgical group: F(1,14)=0.467, p=0.505; main effect of phase: F(1,14)=0.087, p=0.773; surgical group × phase: F(1,14)=1.836, p=0.197; Figure 6C, see Figure 6—source data 3 for raw data).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Orchiectomized rats showed no differences in latencies to press levers pre-surgery.
source: While there were no differences in latencies to press levers pre-surgery (main effect of lever: F(1,7)=0.340, p=0.578; lever × delay interaction: F(4,28)=2.774, p=0.103)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Latencies to press the large reward lever were significantly greater than those for the small reward lever post-surgery in orchiectomized rats, particularly at the longest delays.
source: latencies to press the large reward lever were significantly greater than those for the small reward lever post-surgery, particularly at the longest delays (main effects of lever: F(1,7)=5.911, p=0.045; lever × delay interaction: F(4,28)=11.501, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Removal of testicular hormones shifts male rats' behavior toward a phenotype more similar to that of gonadally-intact females.
source: Taken together, these data show that removal of testicular hormones shifts male rats' behavior toward a phenotype more similar to that of gonadally-intact females, such that both impulsive choice and delay intolerance are increased.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the orchiectomy experiments comparing male behavior to female behavior.

claim: Female rats are markedly more impulsive in their choices than males, preferring small, immediate over larger delayed rewards.
source: Relative to males, female rats were markedly more impulsive in their choices, preferring small, immediate over larger delayed rewards.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main experimental finding.

claim: The sex difference in impulsive choice was not due to differences in reward magnitude discrimination.
source: This effect was not due to differences in reward magnitude discrimination, as both males and females consistently chose the large reward when there was no delay to its delivery.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing both sexes chose the large reward at zero delay.

claim: The sex difference in impulsive choice was not due to differences in task engagement.
source: The effect was also not due to differences in task engagement (free-choice trial omissions)
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on trial omissions.

claim: The sex difference in impulsive choice was not due to differences in hunger-dependent states between males and females.
source: nor to differences in hunger-dependent states between males and females, as ad libitum feeding prior to testing did not alter the observed sex differences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ad libitum feeding experiments.

claim: Female rats are much less tolerant of delays than males.
source: Instead, the current data are consistent with the interpretation that female rats are much less tolerant of delays than males.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on choice behavior and response latencies.

claim: Sex-dependent effects in impulsive choice were not influenced by removal of ovarian hormones.
source: Importantly, while these sex-dependent effects were not influenced by removal of ovarian hormones
evidence: This is a summary of the ovariectomy experimental results.

claim: Removal of testicular hormones resulted in greater impulsive choice in male rats.
source: removal of testicular hormones resulted in greater impulsive choice in male rats
evidence: This is a summary of the orchiectomy experimental results.

claim: Testicular but not ovarian hormones play a critical role in maintenance of sex-typical patterns of impulsive choice.
source: indicating a critical role for testicular but not ovarian hormones in maintenance of sex-typical patterns of impulsive choice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gonadectomy experiments in both sexes.

claim: Response latencies may provide insight into the affective and/or motivational processing underlying a response.
source: Response latencies may provide insight into the affective and/or motivational processing underlying a response; longer latencies may indicate negative affect or reduced motivation for an action, whereas shorter response latencies may indicate positive affect or heightened motivation (Crespi, 1942; Amsel, 1950; Setlow et al., 2003; Mai et al., 2012; Orsini et al., 2015; Shimp et al., 2015; Hernandez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Both males and females had shorter latencies to respond for the large reward relative to the small reward under no delay conditions.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, both males and females in the current study had shorter latencies to respond for the large reward relative to the small reward under no delay conditions
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on response latencies.

claim: Large reward response latencies in both sexes increased as delays to the large reward increased.
source: and large reward response latencies in both sexes increased as delays to the large reward increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on response latencies.

claim: Relative to males, females took significantly longer in responding to the large reward in the presence of delays.
source: Relative to males, however, females took significantly longer in responsding to the large reward in the presence of delays.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on response latencies shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Females displayed an increase in the number of omitted large reward forced-choice trials in the presence of the longest delays.
source: Females also displayed an increase in the number of omitted large reward forced-choice trials in the presence of the longest delays, consistent with delay intolerance (i.e., at those delays, the large reward was so reduced in value as to not be worth pursuing at all).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on trial omissions shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Females were not less sensitive to reward than males.
source: The current data indicate, however, that females were not less sensitive to reward than males.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing females responded as rapidly as males at zero delay.

claim: Females responded as rapidly as males in the absence of a delay.
source: Indeed, females responded as rapidly as males in the absence of a delay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on response latencies.

claim: Females and males are similarly sensitive to reward magnitude but females are substantially less tolerant of delays compared to males.
source: Hence, at least in the context of the food rewards and delays employed here, females and males are similarly sensitive to reward magnitude but females are substantially less tolerant of delays compared to males.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on choice behavior and response latencies.

claim: Females are more sensitive to punishment than males across species.
source: Interestingly, these results parallel findings from across species that females are more sensitive to punishment than males (Miettunen et al., 2007; Rood et al., 2009; Cross et al., 2011; Orsini et al., 2016; Chowdhury et al., 2019; Grissom and Reyes, 2019; Liley et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Females may perceive the delays in the intertemporal choice task as a form of 'cost' that shares overlapping features with explicit punishment.
source: In this context, females may perceive the delays in the intertemporal choice task as a form of 'cost' that shares overlapping features with explicit punishment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Delay intolerance in females as a primary driver of sex differences in intertemporal choice could account for some of the disparate findings in the rodent literature.
source: Delay intolerance in females as a primary driver of sex differences in intertemporal choice could account for some of the disparate findings in the rodent literature.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in relation to prior literature.

claim: Several prior studies failed to detect sex differences on intertemporal choice tasks.
source: Several prior studies failed to detect sex differences on intertemporal choice tasks (Perry et al., 2008; Sackett et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The relatively long delays employed in the present study may have been optimal for detecting sex differences driven by delay intolerance.
source: In particular, the relatively long delays employed in the present study (0–60 s) may have been optimal for detecting sex differences driven by delay intolerance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why the current study detected sex differences.

claim: Several studies using shorter delays failed to detect sex differences.
source: Indeed, several studies using shorter delays (0–40 s or 0–20 s) failed to detect sex differences (Eubig et al., 2014; Sackett et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Small group sizes in prior studies could account for their failure to detect significant sex effects.
source: These studies, however, employed relatively small group sizes (n = 6–9/sex) compared to the current study (n = 16/sex), which could account in part for their failure to detect significant sex effects.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why prior studies did not detect sex differences.

claim: Impulsive choice in both sexes decreases from adolescence to young adulthood.
source: Impulsive choice in both sexes is reported to decrease from adolescence (younger than 2 months) to young adulthood (greater than 2 months; Doremus-Fitzwater et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In male rats, impulsive choice decreases further from 6 months to 24 months.
source: and in male rats it decreases further from 6 months to 24 months (Simon et al., 2010; Hernandez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is possible that sex differences in impulsive choice become more pronounced over the course of young adulthood.
source: Thus, it is possible that sex differences in impulsive choice become more pronounced over the course of young adulthood.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: It is possible that sex differences in impulsive choice are particularly pronounced in Fischer 344 × Brown Norway F1 hybrid rats.
source: Finally, it should be noted that previous studies have not evaluated sex differences in intertemporal choice in Fischer 344 × Brown Norway F1 hybrid rats, and thus it is possible that sex differences are particularly pronounced in this strain.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Sex differences in many aspects of cognition have been observed in several rat strains.
source: Sex differences in many aspects of cognition (including other forms of cost-benefit decision making) have been observed in several rat strains (van den Bos et al., 2012; Peak et al., 2015; Orsini et al., 2016; Blaes et al., 2019; Liley et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several studies have shown differences in impulsive choice between rat strains.
source: and several studies have shown differences in impulsive choice between rat strains (Huskinson et al., 2012; Garcia and Kirkpatrick, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: No studies have directly compared sex differences in impulsive choice between strains.
source: To our knowledge, however, no studies have directly compared sex differences in impulsive choice between strains, suggesting that this will be an important avenue of future research.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature and a suggestion for future research.

claim: Prior studies have reported that the degree of food restriction can affect impulsive choice.
source: Prior studies have reported that the degree of food restriction can affect impulsive choice (Bradshaw and Szabadi, 1992; Wogar et al., 1992; Ho et al., 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Greater food restriction leads to lower levels of impulsive choice.
source: such that greater restriction leads to lower levels of impulsive choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Manipulation of restriction level through ad libitum feeding modestly decreased choices of large, delayed rewards, but this effect did not differ by sex.
source: Manipulation of restriction level through ad libitum feeding modestly decreased choices of large, delayed rewards, but this effect did not differ by sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the ad libitum feeding experiments.

claim: There was a similar increase in the overall number of free-choice trial omissions in males and females under satiated conditions.
source: Additionally, although more females than males omitted entire blocks of free-choice trials under satiated conditions, there was a similar increase in the overall number of free-choice trial omissions in males and females, suggesting that both sexes experienced a comparable degree of satiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on trial omissions under ad libitum feeding.

claim: There is evidence that impulsive choice in women varies across the menstrual cycle.
source: There is evidence that impulsive choice in women varies across the menstrual cycle, suggesting that preference for small, immediate vs. large, delayed rewards can be modulated by fluctuations in ovarian hormones within the physiological range (Kaighobadi and Stevens, 2013; Smith et al., 2014; Diekhof, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some aspects of cognition and behavior in rats can fluctuate across the estrous cycle.
source: Although previous work shows that some aspects of cognition and behavior in rats can fluctuate across the estrous cycle (Shansky et al., 2006; Tuscher et al., 2015; Becker and Koob, 2016; Blume et al., 2017; Pellman et al., 2017; Yagi et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Estrous cycle does not modulate choice behavior in decision making involving risk of punishment or delayed punishment.
source: This finding is consistent with those from previous studies of sex differences in decision making involving risk of punishment or delayed punishment, in which estrous cycle does not modulate choice behavior (Orsini et al., 2016; Liley et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Estrous phase does not influence rats' accuracy in a delayed response working memory task.
source: Similarly, estrous phase does not influence rats' accuracy in a delayed response working memory task, performance on which is correlated with impulsive choice (Shimp et al., 2015; Blaes et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Removal of ovarian hormones through ovariectomy can alter some forms of learning and memory.
source: Removal of ovarian hormones through ovariectomy can alter some forms of learning and memory (Bimonte-Nelson et al., 2003; Qu et al., 2013; Frick et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A study in rats performing an effort-based decision-making task found that ovariectomy increased rats' choice of large, high-effort over small, low-effort rewards relative to their pre-surgery performance.
source: and a study in rats performing an effort-based decision-making task found that ovariectomy increased rats' choice of large, high-effort over small, low-effort rewards relative to their pre-surgery performance (Uban et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: If ovarian hormones contribute to the greater impulsive choice observed in females, their effects may be organizational rather than activational.
source: Consistent with the absence of estrous cycle effects on choice behavior, ovariectomies did not alter task performance, suggesting that if ovarian hormones contribute to the greater impulsive choice observed in females, their effects may be organizational rather than activational.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the ovariectomy results.

claim: Local androgen synthesis in the brain might compensate for loss of circulating ovarian hormones to allow maintenance of pre-surgical patterns of choice behavior in females.
source: Alternatively, local androgen synthesis in the brain (Tobiansky et al., 2018) might compensate for loss of circulating ovarian hormones to allow maintenance of pre-surgical patterns of choice behavior in females.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the ovariectomy results.

claim: Orchiectomy causes a shift toward reduced tolerance for delayed rewards.
source: Analyses of response latencies and trial omissions on forced-choice trials revealed patterns of performance in orchiectomized rats more akin to those in female rats than intact males (i.e., longer response latencies and more trial omissions at longer delays), suggesting that orchiectomy causes a shift toward reduced tolerance for delayed rewards.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on orchiectomized rats.

claim: The effects of orchiectomy on impulsive choice are not explained simply by motivational deficits.
source: Importantly, these results are not explained simply by motivational deficits, as orchiectomies did not increase omissions on free-choice trials.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on trial omissions.

claim: A supraphysiological dose of testosterone administered to intact male rats caused a decrease in impulsive choice.
source: These findings are consistent with the results of a prior study in which a supraphysiological dose of testosterone administered to intact male rats caused a decrease in impulsive choice (Wood et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Testicular hormone signaling may allow bidirectional modulation of impulsive choice in adult rats.
source: Hence, testicular hormone signaling may allow bidirectional modulation of impulsive choice in adult rats.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the orchiectomy results and prior research on testosterone administration.

claim: Testicular hormones do not solely contribute to the male-typical pattern of impulsive choice in an organizational manner, but play an activational role as well.
source: The fact that orchiectomy shifted impulsive choice implies that testicular hormones do not solely contribute to the male-typical pattern of impulsive choice in an organizational manner, but that they play an activational role as well.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the orchiectomy results.

claim: Impulsive choice is mediated by a network of corticolimbic-basal ganglia structures, including prefrontal cortex, basolateral amygdala, and nucleus accumbens, as well as dopaminergic and serotonergic innervation of these structures.
source: Impulsive choice is mediated by a network of corticolimbic-basal ganglia structures, including prefrontal cortex, basolateral amygdala, and nucleus accumbens, as well as dopaminergic and serotonergic innervation of these structures (see Floresco et al., 2008; Peters and Büchel, 2011; Bailey et al., 2016; Fobbs and Mizumori, 2017; Frost and McNaughton, 2017 for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Androgen receptors are found within brain regions that mediate impulsive choice, and their functions can be modulated by manipulations of testicular hormones.
source: Androgen receptors are found within all of these brain regions, and their functions can be modulated by manipulations of testicular hormones (Tobiansky et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: It is likely that the effects of orchiectomy on impulsive choice are mediated at least in part via hormonal effects on brain systems that mediate impulsive choice.
source: Hence, it is likely that the effects of orchiectomy on impulsive choice are mediated at least in part via hormonal effects on these brain systems.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on knowledge of androgen receptors in relevant brain regions.

claim: There was a significant and robust difference in impulsive choice between males and females that was not readily attributable to differences in food motivation or reward sensitivity.
source: First, there was a significant and robust difference in impulsive choice between males and females that was not readily attributable to differences in food motivation or reward sensitivity.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Testicular hormones are necessary for maintaining the bias toward delayed gratification typical of males.
source: Second, we describe the novel finding that testicular hormones are necessary for maintaining the bias toward delayed gratification typical of males
evidence: This is a summary statement of the orchiectomy findings.

claim: Ovarian hormones do not appear to be necessary for maintaining the female-typical bias toward immediate gratification.
source: whereas ovarian hormones do not appear to be necessary for maintaining the female-typical bias toward immediate gratification.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the ovariectomy findings.

claim: The robust differences between males and females, as well as the differential roles of gonadal hormones, highlight the importance of assessing both sexes in studies of cost-benefit decision making.
source: Finally, the robust differences between males and females, as well as the differential roles of gonadal hormones, highlight the importance of assessing both sexes in studies of cost-benefit decision making (see van den Bos et al., 2013; Orsini and Setlow, 2017 for reviews).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for future research.

claim: The current study had some of the largest group sizes to date in an assessment of sex differences in impulsive choice.
source: The current study had some of the largest group sizes to date in an assessment of sex differences in impulsive choice
evidence: This is a statement about the study design.

claim: The study is limited in that rats of only a single strain and age were evaluated on a single task design using a fixed set of delays.
source: however, it is limited in that rats of only a single strain and age were evaluated on a single task design using a fixed set of delays.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: It is not clear to what extent the current results are representative of human behavior.
source: As such, although the use of rodents avoids factors that can bias studies of impulsive choice in human subjects (such as age, education, and socioeconomic status), it is not clear to what extent the current results are representative of human behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of generalizing from rodent to human behavior.

claim: A meta-analysis of studies assessing impulsive choice in human subjects found no sex difference.
source: Indeed, a meta-analysis of studies assessing impulsive choice in human subjects found no sex difference, although the heterogeneity in subject ages and task designs renders it challenging to draw generalities (Cross et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In both rodents and humans, females appear to be more sensitive than males to punishment.
source: Particularly given that (in both rodents and humans) females appear to be more sensitive than males to punishment (Cross et al., 2011; Orsini and Setlow, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Greater impulsive choice among females may be most evident in circumstances involving actual (experienced, rather than hypothetical) rewards and delays.
source: it may be the case that greater impulsive choice among females will be most evident in circumstances involving actual (experienced, rather than hypothetical) rewards and delays.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about when sex differences might be most evident.

claim: The sex differences observed in the study (greater impulsive choice in females than males) are opposite of those predicted by the sex prevalence of psychiatric disorders associated with alterations in impulsive choice such as ADHD, SUDs, and anorexia nervosa.
source: Notably, the sex differences observed here (greater impulsive choice in females than males) are opposite of those predicted by the sex prevalence of psychiatric disorders associated with alterations in impulsive choice such as ADHD, SUDs, and anorexia nervosa.
evidence: This is an observation about the relationship between the findings and psychiatric disorder prevalence.

claim: Male-prevalent psychiatric disorders are associated with male-atypical patterns of impulsive choice.
source: In other words (and if the present findings in rats were extended to humans) male-prevalent psychiatric disorders are associated with male-atypical patterns of impulsive choice
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the relationship between the findings and psychiatric disorders.

claim: Female-prevalent psychiatric disorders are associated with female-atypical patterns of impulsive choice.
source: whereas female-prevalent psychiatric disorders are associated with female-atypical patterns of impulsive choice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the relationship between the findings and psychiatric disorders.

claim: It is not clear whether and how the relationships between sex-typical impulsive choice and psychiatric disorders are relevant to the etiology or symptoms of psychiatric disorders.
source: Although it is not clear whether and how such relationships are relevant to the etiology or symptoms of psychiatric disorders, future studies employing more targeted manipulations of gonadal hormone signaling may begin to address these questions.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current findings and suggestions for future research.

claim: Adult male and female Fischer 344 × Brown Norway F1 hybrid rats were obtained at 6 months of age from the National Institute on Aging colony.
source: Adult male (n = 16) and female (n = 16) Fischer 344 × Brown Norway F1 hybrid (FBN) rats were obtained at 6 months of age from the National Institute on Aging colony (Charles River Laboratories)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Rats were individually housed in the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care International-accredited vivarium facility.
source: and individually housed in the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care International-accredited vivarium facility in the McKnight Brain Institute building at the University of Florida.
evidence: This is a description of the housing conditions.

claim: The study was performed in strict accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health.
source: This study was performed in strict accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: All animal procedures were conducted according to protocols approved by the University of Florida Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All animal procedures were conducted according to protocols approved by the University of Florida Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol # 201904961).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: The facility was maintained at a consistent temperature of 25° with a 12 hr light/dark cycle.
source: The facility was maintained at a consistent temperature of 25° with a 12 hr light/dark cycle (lights on at 0700)
evidence: This is a description of the housing conditions.

claim: Rats were acclimated in the facility and handled for at least one week prior to initiation of any procedures.
source: Rats were acclimated in this facility and handled for at least one week prior to initiation of any procedures.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: Group sizes were based on previous work that assessed sex differences in decision making and PFC-dependent cognition.
source: Group sizes were based on previous work from our labs that has assessed sex differences in decision making and PFC-dependent cognition (Orsini et al., 2016; Blaes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for group sizes.

claim: In previous work, n = 8 rats/sex was determined to be needed to detect sex differences.
source: In this work, n = 8 rats/sex was determined to be needed to detect sex differences.
evidence: This is a statement about power analysis from prior work.

claim: Group sizes of n = 16/sex were employed to have sufficient rats of each sex for both GDX and sham conditions.
source: Group sizes of n = 16/sex were employed to have sufficient rats of each sex for both GDX and sham conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for group sizes.

claim: Rats were tested in three separate cohorts, each separated by 6–12 months.
source: Rats were tested in three separate cohorts, each separated by 6–12 months.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The intertemporal choice task was based on a design by Evenden and Ryan, 1996.
source: The intertemporal choice task was based on a design by Evenden and Ryan, 1996
evidence: This is a statement about the task design.

claim: The intertemporal choice task was used previously to demonstrate age-related alterations in decision making in both Fischer 344 and FBN rats.
source: and was used previously to demonstrate age-related alterations in decision making in both Fischer 344 (Simon et al., 2010) and FBN (Hernandez et al., 2017) rats.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.
